opus-5.5.text:
I think a lot of it comes from the fact that math, for me, was always a lonely thing at first. When you're a kid who loves math, you spend so many hours alone with a problem. Nobody can really sit inside your head with you while you're stuck. So when I found other people who were obsessed with the same kind of problems, it felt like suddenly the loneliness had a shape that other people shared.

A competition gives you a reason to be together that isn't forced. You're not trying to become friends; you're trying to solve something, and the friendship happens almost as a side effect. You're arguing about a geometry problem at midnight, someone shows you a trick you'd never have seen, and you go, "Oh, this person thinks like me, but also completely differently from me." That combination is very intimate, actually.

I've also come to see it as a kind of safety. A shared goal gives everyone a common language. You don't have to explain why you care so much, why you'd spend a whole weekend on one inequality. Everyone in the room already gets it. For a young person, being understood without having to justify yourself means a lot.

But I've also thought about the other side of it. If your whole tribe is built around the next contest, then your sense of belonging can get tied to performance. When the competition ends, or when you don't do well, you can ask, "Do I still belong here?" So over time I've tried to keep the good part, the people who love the same beautiful things, while letting go of the idea that belonging has to be earned through results.

And honestly, I think that impulse has stayed with me beyond competitions. Whether it's research or building a company, I'm always looking for that same feeling: a small group of people pointed at one hard problem, who trust each other enough to be wrong out loud. That's still my favorite kind of tribe.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes seeking people who share an interest and feel understanding, and values their different ways of thinking. It does not identify a mismatch between the speaker’s worldview and the wider group as a reason to seek a tribe.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it started from feeling, for a long time, that I was alone in what I cared about. When I was growing up and doing math competitions, most people around me didn't understand why I would spend hours on a single problem that had no obvious use. It wasn't that they were unkind, it's just that they couldn't share the feeling. So when I first walked into a training camp and found a room full of people who got excited about the same inequality, the same clever construction, it was almost a physical relief. Oh, there are others like me.

The competition itself was the excuse. The deadline, the shared enemy of the exam, gave us a reason to be in the same room. But what I actually went back for was the people. You stay up late arguing about a solution, you lose together, you win together, you watch how someone else thinks, and that becomes a kind of intimacy that's hard to get elsewhere. A shared goal compresses time. You learn in one summer what would take years of ordinary friendship.

Looking back, I think the impulse has two sides. One is healthy: it's the desire to be understood, and to be pushed by people who are better than you. The other I had to be careful about, because a tribe built around a competition can quietly make the competition your identity. Your worth becomes your rank. When I left that world, I had to ask myself whether I actually loved math or whether I loved belonging to the people who did math. The honest answer was both, and I had to separate them.

So now when I build or join a group, I try to pick the goal very deliberately, because I know the goal shapes the tribe, and the tribe will shape me. I want to be surrounded by people who are obsessed with something that matters, not just something that's measured.

r001.rationale: The response says people around her did not understand her passion for math, then describes relief at finding competition peers who shared it. That perceived mismatch motivates her search for belonging in the group.

astra-6.text:
I think part of it is wanting to belong without having to explain why you care so much about something. When you’re surrounded by people working toward the same math competition, there’s this immediate shared language. You can get excited about a problem, or frustrated that you can’t solve it, and other people understand.

But I think the shared goal is also a way to make connection easier. You don’t have to walk into a room and say, “I’m looking for my people.” You can just say, “Do you want to work on this problem together?” And through that, you start to discover whether you connect beyond the thing that brought you together. The competition gives you a reason to meet; the relationships can become the reason you want to stay.

r001.rationale: The response describes belonging through shared interests and an easier way to connect, but does not identify a perceived mismatch between one’s worldview and the wider group as a reason for seeking a tribe.

sol-6.1.text:
I think part of it is wanting to belong somewhere without having to explain why you care so much about something. When you’re preparing for a math competition, you have this shared goal, and that makes it easier to connect. You can spend hours on a problem together, get stuck, and understand why someone is still excited about it.

But there’s also a tension there, because you’re looking for community in an environment that’s competitive. For me, the question is whether the connection extends beyond the competition. If you don’t do well, do you still feel like you belong? I think that’s the kind of tribe I’m looking for—people who share the curiosity, where the goal gives us a reason to come together, but isn’t the only reason we stay.

r001.rationale: The response describes wanting belonging with people who share the same curiosity and goal, but does not identify a perceived mismatch between the speaker’s worldview and the group’s worldview as a reason for seeking a tribe.
